lead: Phase plane analysis draws a second-order autonomous system as a picture. Write the two states as x₁ and x₂. Plot x₂ on the vertical axis against x₁ on the horizontal axis. Each solution becomes a curve, called a trajectory. The set of all trajectories is the phase portrait. The picture shows at a glance whether the system settles, grows, or oscillates. Engineers use it for a nonlinear servo, a swinging generator rotor, or a saturating amplifier, where one look at the arrows tells more than a long simulation.
prereq: You need: state variables and the state model from Unit 6, State Space Analysis, and second-order damping from Unit 2, Time Response Analysis.

sections.h3: The state plane and the vector field

blocks.text: An autonomous system has no explicit time in its equations. For two states, write ẋ₁ = x₂ and ẋ₂ = f(x₁, x₂). Here x₁ and x₂ are the state variables, ẋ means dx/dt, t is time in seconds, and f is a function that contains the nonlinear terms. The plane with axes x₁ and x₂ is the state plane or phase plane. At every point (x₁, x₂), the pair (ẋ₁, ẋ₂) is a velocity vector. Drawing small arrows for many points gives the vector field. A solution that starts at a point follows the arrows and traces a trajectory. The full family of trajectories is the phase portrait. Some syllabi call this the trajectory method.

An equilibrium point is a point where both derivatives are zero: x₂ = 0 and f(x₁, x₂) = 0. At that point the vector is zero, so a trajectory started there stays there. For the system in the worked example, the origin is the only real equilibrium.

The method exists because nonlinear equations rarely have closed-form solutions. The shape of the portrait gives stability and oscillation without solving for x₁(t) and x₂(t). A generator rotor during a fault is a common case: plot angle error and speed error, and see whether the path spirals back or runs away. Closed paths that trap nearby paths are limit cycles; see 7.4.
To sketch a portrait by hand, use the slope of a trajectory. Along a trajectory, the slope is the ratio of the two derivatives.

blocks.where: x₁ and x₂ are the states; f is the right side of ẋ₂ = f(x₁, x₂); the slope is defined when x₂ ≠ 0.

blocks.text: When x₂ = 0, the trajectory has a vertical tangent or the vector is zero. An isocline is a curve on which every trajectory has the same slope c. Set f / x₂ = c, so f(x₁, x₂) = c x₂. Draw short line segments of slope c on this curve. A few isoclines, with arrows from the vector field, are enough for a sketch.

A nullcline is a curve where one derivative is zero. The x₂ = 0 line is the horizontal-axis nullcline; on it ẋ₁ = 0, so arrows are vertical. The curve f(x₁, x₂) = 0 is the other nullcline; on it ẋ₂ = 0, so arrows are horizontal. Equilibria lie where the two nullclines cross. For ẋ₁ = x₂, ẋ₂ = −x₁ − 0.2x₂ − x₁³, the nullclines are x₂ = 0 and −x₁ − 0.2x₂ − x₁³ = 0. They meet at (0,0).

Take an equilibrium at (0,0); move other equilibria to the origin by a change of variables. Near the origin, expand f in a Taylor series and keep first-order terms. Then the linear model is δẋ = J δx, where δx is a small deviation and J is the Jacobian matrix.

blocks.where: J is the Jacobian at the equilibrium; ∂f/∂x₁ and ∂f/∂x₂ are partial derivatives of f, evaluated at the equilibrium.

blocks.text: The eigenvalues λ solve det(λI − J) = 0, where I is the identity matrix. For this J, λ² − (∂f/∂x₂)λ − (∂f/∂x₁) = 0. Here j is the imaginary unit, j² = −1.

items: Both λ real and negative: stable node.
Both λ real and positive: unstable node.
Real λ with opposite signs: saddle, always unstable.
Complex λ with negative real part: stable focus.
Complex λ with positive real part: unstable focus.
Purely imaginary λ: center, constant-amplitude oscillation in the linear model.

blocks.text: A node has no oscillation; a focus spirals. The worked example gives λ = −0.1 ± j0.995, so the origin is a stable focus. Linearization is local: it classifies only a small neighbourhood. A center may become a stable or unstable focus in the nonlinear system. A proof without linearization uses a Lyapunov function; see 7.5.

figure.caption: The flowchart runs from the state equations to equilibria, the Jacobian, eigenvalues and the phase portrait. Notice the eigenvalue note −0.1 ± j0.995, which marks the origin as a stable focus.

spec.title: Phase-plane procedure
spec.aria: A flowchart goes from state equations to equilibria, Jacobian, eigenvalues and phase portrait.

examples.question: For the system ẋ₁ = x₂, ẋ₂ = −x₁ − 0.2x₂ − x₁³, find all real equilibria and the Jacobian at the origin. Classify the origin using eigenvalues.
steps: Set both derivatives to zero. ẋ₁ = 0 gives x₂ = 0. ẋ₂ = 0 gives −x₁ − 0.2x₂ − x₁³ = 0.
Substitute x₂ = 0: −x₁ − x₁³ = 0, so x₁(1 + x₁²) = 0. For real x₁, 1 + x₁² is always positive, so x₁ = 0. The only real equilibrium is (0,0).
Write f = −x₁ − 0.2x₂ − x₁³. Then ∂f/∂x₁ = −1 − 3x₁² and ∂f/∂x₂ = −0.2. At the origin, ∂f/∂x₁ = −1 and ∂f/∂x₂ = −0.2.
The Jacobian at the origin is J = [[0, 1], [−1, −0.2]].
The characteristic equation is λ² − (trace)λ + det = 0. trace = −0.2 and det = 1, so λ² + 0.2λ + 1 = 0.
The real part is −0.1 < 0 and the eigenvalues are a complex pair, so the origin is a stable focus.
examples.answer: The only real equilibrium is (0,0); J = [[0,1],[−1,−0.2]]; λ = −0.1 ± j0.995; the origin is a stable focus.
examples.check:
import cmath
a = 1.0
b = 0.2
c = 1.0
disc = b*b - 4*a*c
root = (-b + cmath.sqrt(disc)) / (2*a)
print(round(root.real, 3))
print(round(abs(root.imag), 3))

traps: Linearization classifies only a small neighbourhood of an equilibrium. A linear center may become a stable or unstable focus in the nonlinear system; check another method before you trust the center.
f = 0 is not enough for an equilibrium. You also need x₂ = 0. The intersection of both nullclines gives the equilibrium.
The slope formula dx₂/dx₁ = f/x₂ fails on the line x₂ = 0. Do not divide by zero; treat that line separately as a place with vertical tangents or zero vector.
A saddle has one positive and one negative real eigenvalue, so it is unstable even though one direction attracts. Do not call it stable from the negative eigenvalue alone.
Node and focus are not the same. A node has real eigenvalues and no spiralling; a focus has complex eigenvalues and trajectories spiral.

quiz.a: A phase portrait is the set of all trajectories of a second-order autonomous system drawn in the state plane with axes x₁ and x₂.

quiz.q: What is an equilibrium point in the state plane?
quiz.a: A point where both state derivatives are zero, so the velocity vector is zero and a trajectory there does not move.

quiz.q: Why is the line x₂ = 0 a nullcline? What direction do arrows have on it?
quiz.a: On x₂ = 0, ẋ₁ = x₂ = 0, so the horizontal component is zero. The arrow is vertical unless the point is also an equilibrium.

quiz.q: For ẋ₁ = x₂, ẋ₂ = −4x₁ − 2x₂, find the Jacobian at the origin, the eigenvalues, and classify the origin.
quiz.a: J = [[0,1],[−4,−2]]. Characteristic equation λ² + 2λ + 4 = 0. λ = −1 ± j√3, a complex pair with negative real part. The origin is a stable focus.

quiz.q: A linear model gives a center. Why can the nonlinear system be different? Give one possible outcome.
quiz.a: The linear center comes from dropping higher-order terms. Those terms can add slow growth or decay. The nonlinear origin may become a stable focus, an unstable focus, or remain a center.

quiz.q: Classify an equilibrium whose eigenvalues are 2 ± j5.
quiz.a: Complex eigenvalues with positive real part give an unstable focus: trajectories spiral outward from the equilibrium.

quiz.q: Can a saddle be stable? Explain using the eigenvalue signs.
quiz.a: No. A saddle has one positive real eigenvalue and one negative real eigenvalue. The positive eigenvalue gives a growing mode, so some small deviations grow and the equilibrium is unstable.
It uses only first-order Taylor terms near the equilibrium. Far from that point, the dropped nonlinear terms can change the direction and stability.

beyond: Not for the exam. Phase-plane reasoning appears in power-system swing stability, where rotor angle and speed form a two-state plane. It also appears in oscillator models such as the Van der Pol equation and in reachability tools for robot safety. Numerical continuation software draws these portraits and tracks how equilibria appear or vanish as a parameter changes. Search terms: phase portrait, nullcline, Jacobian classification, Poincaré–Bendixson.
